questions.question: A life currently aged $x$ has random remaining lifetime $T_x$. Its curtate future lifetime is $K_x=\lfloor T_x\rfloor$. What does this quantity describe?
options: The expected number of complete future years, rounded down.
The random number of complete future years that the life survives.
The age at death, rounded down to an integer age.
The number of future years begun, including the final incomplete year.

questions.question: For a nonnegative continuous future lifetime $T$, let $K=\lfloor T\rfloor$. What does observing $K=0$ tell us about the time of death?
options: Death occurs exactly at the current instant.
The life completes one year before death.
The exact time of death is known to be half a year away.
Death occurs before completing the first future year.

questions.question: Let $T$ be a nonnegative absolutely continuous future lifetime with survivor $S(t)=\mathbb{P}(T>t)$, and $K=\lfloor T\rfloor$. For integer $k\ge0$, which formula gives $\mathbb{P}(K>k)$ for every such lifetime law?
options: $\mathbb{P}(T=k)$.

questions.question: A continuous lifetime $T$ has density $f(t)$, and $K=\lfloor T\rfloor$. Why is $f(k)$ generally not the probability $\mathbb{P}(K=k)$ for an integer $k\ge0$?
options: The two are equal because each curtate bin has length one.
The probability is the density value at k+1 instead.
A pointwise density is not the probability of the whole one-year bin.
The probability is the reciprocal of the density value at k.

questions.question: Let $K=\lfloor T\rfloor$ for an absolutely continuous lifetime $T$. For integer $k\ge0$, why may $\mathbb{P}(T\ge k)$ be replaced by $\mathbb{P}(T>k)$ when finding $\mathbb{P}(K\ge k)$?
options: The two lifetime events are identical as sets.
The lifetime assigns probability zero to the single point k.
The floor removes every observation exactly at an integer.
Every integer death time is shifted forward by one year.

questions.question: For a continuous future lifetime $T$, survivor probabilities are $\mathbb{P}(T>2)=0.6$ and $\mathbb{P}(T>3)=0.4$. With $K=\lfloor T\rfloor$, what is $\mathbb{P}(K=2)$?

A life has probability $0.8$ of surviving two more years. Conditional on that survival, its probability of dying in the next year is $0.25$. For curtate lifetime $K=\lfloor T\rfloor$, what is $\mathbb{P}(K=2)$?
For a continuous lifetime $T$, survival at times $1,2,3$ is $0.8,0.5,0.2$, and survival at time $4$ is zero. With $K=\lfloor T\rfloor$, what is $\mathbb{E}[K]$?
Let $K=\lfloor T\rfloor$ for a nonnegative continuous lifetime $T$ with survivor $S(t)$. For a real number $r$ with $k\le r<k+1$ and integer $k\ge0$, which formula gives the CDF $\mathbb{P}(K\le r)$?

A life has continuous remaining lifetime $T$ and curtate value $K=\lfloor T\rfloor$. It survives an integer number $m\ge1$ of further years. On the event $T>m$, what is the curtate value of its new remaining duration $T-m$?
A continuous lifetime $T$ has survival probabilities $0.8,0.5,0.2$ at times $1,2,3$ and zero at time $4$. For $K=\lfloor T\rfloor$, what is the second moment $\mathbb{E}[K^2]$?
A future lifetime $T$ is uniform on $(0,2.5)$ years, and $K=\lfloor T\rfloor$. What is $\mathbb{P}(K=2)$?

Two absolutely continuous lifetimes have densities $f_A(t)=1$ and $f_B(t)=2t$ on $(0,1)$, respectively, and zero outside. Define $K_A=\lfloor T_A\rfloor$ and $K_B=\lfloor T_B\rfloor$. What does this pair show about curtate information?
options: Equal curtate laws imply equal continuous lifetime laws.
The two curtate laws differ because their density shapes differ.
Their half-year survival probabilities agree because the bin length is one.
Equal curtate laws can hide different half-year survival probabilities.

questions.question: A life survives $s$ years, where $0<s<1$. Its original duration is $T>s$, curtate count is $K=\lfloor T\rfloor$, and fractional part is $U=T-K$. How is the new curtate count $\lfloor T-s\rfloor$ determined?
options: $K$ in both cases.
$K$ if $U\ge s$, and $K-1$ if $U<s$.
$K-1$ in both cases.
$K-1$ if $U\ge s$, and $K$ if $U<s$.

questions.question: A proposed continuous lifetime model gives its curtate count $K=\lfloor T\rfloor$ moments $\mathbb{E}[K]=0.6$ and $\mathbb{E}[K^2]=0.5$. Which check correctly rules out the proposed pair?
options: The second moment is smaller than the mean, despite $K^2\ge K$.
The mean of an integer-valued count must itself be an integer.
The second moment must always equal the square of the mean.
No check rules it out because both proposed moments are nonnegative.

questions.question: A continuous lifetime has curtate count $K=\lfloor T\rfloor$ with masses $0.2,0.3,0.5$ at $0,1,2$. No fractional interpolation is specified. Which interval is exactly the possible range of $\mathbb{P}(K\ge2\mid T>1.5)$?
